hook_angle: Where things stand now: the stratosphere still holds roughly 146 teragrams of water that a single volcano put there in January 2022. Hold on that number, then rewind to 04:16 UTC on 15 January 2022 — the moment the island above the vent stopped existing.
stakes: A kingdom was hit by a tsunami within minutes and a volcano was erased down to a 850 m crater, while the blast punched the atmosphere from the seafloor into the mesosphere — and the water it left behind is still changing the chemistry of the layer that shields you from ultraviolet light.

sections.heading: The setting: a caldera at exactly the wrong depth
sections.claim: Hunga's caldera sat about 150 metres below the surface — shallow enough that erupting magma flashed enormous volumes of seawater to steam, and deep enough that the ocean did not simply smother it. This is the cause the timeline starts from. One caveat: Henley et al. (2024) argue the standard Surtseyan fuel-coolant explanation is not supported by the satellite imagery, and propose a gas-seal and hydraulic-fracture mechanism instead — the disagreement is live.
sections.key_number: about 150 m (490 ft) of water over the caldera
sections.source: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, citing Millán et al., Geophysical Research Letters, 2022

visual.title: THE DEPTH THAT MADE IT EXPLODE
labels: Hunga caldera depth below sea level
visual.source_note: NASA/JPL — Millán et al., Geophys. Res. Lett., 2022

sections.heading: Thirty minutes to the mesosphere
sections.claim: The climactic plume rose from the ocean surface to 58 km in roughly half an hour, an ascent of at least 40 m/s, and a secondary pulse rose above 50 km shortly after — the highest plume in the satellite record. Carr et al.'s stereo retrieval puts the overshooting top at 50–55 km, so 58 km is NASA Langley's figure, not a settled consensus.
sections.key_number: 58 km plume top versus 35 km for Pinatubo (1.5 times the height)
sections.source: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Langley Research Center, GOES-17 and Himawari-8 stereo analysis, February 2022

visual.title: HIGHEST PLUME IN THE SATELLITE RECORD
visual.source_note: NASA Earth Observatory — GOES-17 / Himawari-8 stereo retrievals

sections.heading: The wave that would not stop
sections.claim: The explosion launched a surface-guided Lamb wave — the signature of an atmospheric blast — that circled the Earth four times, plus three antipodal passages, over six days, and produced audible sound more than 10,000 km from the vent. Measured by Lamb-wave amplitude, the Hunga explosion was comparable in size to the 1883 Krakatoa eruption.
sections.key_number: 4 passages around Earth, plus 3 antipodal, in 6 days
sections.source: Science — Matoza et al., 'Atmospheric waves and global seismoacoustic observations of the January 2022 Hunga eruption, Tonga', 2022

visual.title: AROUND THE WORLD, THEN AGAIN, THEN AGAIN
visual.source_note: Matoza et al., Science, 2022 — Lamb wave tracked over 6 days

sections.heading: What it left in the stratosphere, and what is still there
sections.claim: The blast injected around 146 teragrams of water vapour — about 10% of all the water already in the stratosphere and roughly four times the Pinatubo injection — and because the plume was so water-rich, sulfate aerosols formed in days rather than the usual month. In the wettest air, ozone fell by as much as 30%. JPL gives 146 Tg; NOAA's balloon campaign estimated about 150 million tons from the ground — the same event, two instruments, a range rather than a single agreed figure.
sections.source: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (Millán et al., 2022) for 146 Tg; NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory for the 30% ozone loss

visual.title: WATER INJECTED INTO THE STRATOSPHERE
visual.source_note: NASA/JPL (MLS, 2022); Pinatubo value from Communications Earth & Environment, 2022 — a modelling-based estimate, not a measurement

payoff: The core answer is depth plus water plus an open vent: a shallow submarine caldera flash-boiled seawater into steam, the explosion excavated an 850 m deep crater, and because the vent sat under the ocean the blast delivered a water-rich, gas-driven plume straight into the stratosphere and mesosphere in about half an hour — high enough and fast enough that the pressure pulse it made could not dissipate locally, so it wrapped the planet. On how tall it actually was, how violent it was, and what drove it, scientists still disagree: NASA Langley measures the top at 58 km while Carr et al.'s stereo work gives 50–55 km; the Volcanic Explosivity Index is cited as 5.8 in one paper and VEI 6 in another; and Henley et al. argue against the long-assumed phreatomagmatic fuel-coolant mechanism, favouring a gas-sealing and hydraulic-fracture model instead.
takeaway: Hunga Tonga is one of twelve confirmed submarine volcanoes along the Tofua Arc, according to the Smithsonian's Global Volcanism Program — and the water it pushed into the stratosphere is still circulating above you.
